dynamic_range: Dynamic-range definitions: DR1 is peak brightness divided by the median absolute deviation from the image median. A 9 by 9 uvw-facet run reached DR1 = 12,580 and DR2 = 40, with 1,348 s per residual calculation and 30,488 s total. W-projection with 64 w-planes reached higher DR1 = 18,198 and DR2 = 524, with 83 s of kernel initialization, 607 s per residual calculation, and 3,161 s total. Thus this representative higher-dynamic-range w-projection run took about one tenth the total time of the 9 by 9 facet run. At comparable dynamic range it is about an order of magnitude faster than uvw-space faceting. They report about a factor of 30 advantage in residual-calculation time and about a factor of 3 in error performance over facets, both in favor of w-projection; the overall advantage is smaller because faceting can skip empty facets early in CLEAN and has favorable minor-cycle scaling.

dynamic_range: Taylor-order numerical test: Noise-free 8-hour EVLA simulations used a 1 Jy point source with spectral index -1 and no curvature, five bandwidth ratios from 1.1:1 to 3:1 around 2 GHz, natural weighting, at most ten iterations, loop gain 1, and a 1 microJy stopping threshold. For a 2:1 band and four Taylor terms, Figure 4 reports dynamic range of about 100,000, reference-frequency peak-flux error of about 1 part in 1,000, absolute spectral-index error of about 0.01, and absolute curvature error of about 0.1. papers.title: Sparsity Averaging Reweighted Analysis (SARA): a novel algorithm for radio-interferometric imaging

snr: Controlled simulation context: Ground-truth M31 H II-region and 30 Doradus images are each 256 x 256 pixels with normalized brightness in [0.01, 1]. Visibilities follow the discrete measurement model with the primary beam set to identity. Random variable-density masks sample the half Fourier plane more densely at low spatial frequencies, omit the zero-frequency component, and range from 10% to 90% coverage. Complex Gaussian noise is added at 30 dB input SNR. The profiles are generic rather than tied to a telescope or observing frequency, and each plotted mean and one-standard-deviation error bar is computed over 100 simulations.

Reconstruction SNR definition: The quantitative fidelity metric is \(20 \log_{10}(\sigma_x/\sigma_{x-\hat{x}})\) dB, where \(\sigma_x\) is the standard deviation of the ground-truth image and \(\sigma_{x-\hat{x}}\) is the standard deviation of the reconstruction error. Input SNR uses the same form with the per-visibility noise standard deviation in the denominator. This is a ground-truth image-domain error score, not peak-to-RMS image dynamic range.

Coverage sweep: Against the directly run BP, BPDb8, TV, and IUWT benchmarks, SARA has the highest mean reconstruction SNR at every tested coverage for both images. For M31, the paper reports a gain over every other method of more than 6 dB at 10% coverage and at least 3 dB at the remaining coverages. For 30 Doradus, it reports at least a 2 dB gain at every coverage.

Representative 30%-coverage reconstructions: The individual M31 example reports 32.82 dB for BP, 33.70 dB for BPDb8, 32.12 dB for IUWT, 33.89 dB for TV, and 38.43 dB for SARA. The individual 30 Doradus example reports 16.67, 24.53, 17.87, 26.47, and 29.08 dB, respectively. These are example-image values at 30 dB input SNR, not the 100-run mean values digitized from the coverage plots.

Spread-spectrum illustration: A separate Cygnus A simulation uses 30% coverage, 30 dB input SNR, and a random-phase modulation in the measurement operator as a simplified spread-spectrum acquisition. Reported reconstruction SNRs are 16.6 dB for BP, 36.0 dB for BPDb8, 29.9 dB for BPIU, 28.7 dB for TV, and 40.2 dB for SARA. The paper presents this as an illustration, uses random phase rather than a physical quadratic w-term phase, and does not average the result over repeated trials.

Qualitative residual and artifact assessment: Residual images are the difference between the observed dirty image and the dirty image predicted from the reconstruction. SARA is judged to leave fewer background artifacts and smaller structural errors for M31, and to recover both point-like and extended 30 Doradus structure without the spurious points of BP/IUWT or the cartoon-like bias of TV. The paper notes that IUWT can produce a nearly flat residual despite larger ground-truth image error, and that all methods can give noise-like 30 Doradus residuals while differing materially in reconstruction SNR. These are visual assessments, not additional numerical metrics.
runtime: Runtime: MATLAB wall-clock times are measured on a 2.4 GHz Xeon quad-core processor and plotted in log10 seconds over the coverage sweep, again as means and one-standard-deviation error bars over 100 simulations. The paper describes SARA runtime as of the order of minutes and similar to TV in these tests and to published MS-CLEAN times. It does not tabulate exact times, specify the Xeon model, memory, MATLAB version, thread use, or visibility counts, and its MS-CLEAN comparison is cross-paper rather than a controlled same-hardware run.

Scope and missing benchmarks: The study uses synthetic, on-grid discrete Fourier samples and no measured interferometer data. Except for the simplified spread-spectrum illustration, it assumes a small field, identity primary beam, monochromatic non-polarized imaging, and no direction-dependent effects. It does not report flux-recovery error, source completeness, residual RMS in physical units, SSIM, memory use, or a direct CLEAN/MS-CLEAN runtime or fidelity benchmark. The authors identify continuous visibility handling, lower-level implementation, and parallel or distributed solvers as future work.

rdr_residual: MWA Vela/Puppis A residual fidelity: On a real 2 min MWA observation, default CASA multi-scale CLEAN gives 64 mJy/PSF residual RMS, while WSClean with scale-bias 0.60 gives 50 mJy/PSF. The paper attributes this floor to FINUFFT's default type-3 upsampling factor of 1.25, which lowers RAM and FFT size but limits accuracy to about nine digits. Chunked HVOX tracks the same curve but slightly misses the requested target because numerical errors accumulate when chunk outputs are summed; the authors propose compensating by tightening each sub-transform's target according to the number of blocks. NIFTY generally exceeds its requested accuracy by about one order of magnitude, while omitting the w-term in NIFTY 2D produces a much larger error that is insensitive to the requested target.

psnr: PSNR (peak signal-to-noise ratio): used specifically in the model-mismatch/robustness experiment (Fig. 8) to quantify reconstruction quality degradation as the PSF is perturbed by warping distortions γ ∈ [0,30] outside the training distribution (model trained only at γ=0). PSNR degrades predictably with increasing γ, but the authors note this pixel-level metric is more sensitive to model mismatch than actual visual/qualitative reconstruction quality, which remains comparatively stable even at extreme distortion (γ=30) — flagged as a caveat about PSNR's limits as a fidelity proxy under calibration/model-mismatch conditions.

Fine-tuning convergence speed: (efficiency metric, not fidelity per se): under PSF mismatch, fine-tuning an existing POLISH++ model reaches peak PSNR in 11 epochs vs. 57 epochs training from scratch (>5× speedup), both far outperforming the unadapted mismatched baseline.

Comparisons to R2D2 and other DL methods: R2D2 (Aghabiglou et al. 2024) and other prior DL imaging methods (Radionets, Deflation Net, GU-Net, RI-GAN) are compared only via the qualitative capability table (Table 1: max image size, max dynamic range, domain, training data, model-mismatch handling) — POLISH++ is reported as the only method combining large image size (12,960 px vs. 512 px for R2D2), the highest dynamic range (~10^6 vs. 5×10^5 for R2D2), non-Gaussian source morphology (strong lenses), and synthetic PSF model-mismatch testing. iterations: Strong-lens discovery — True Positive Rate (TPR) at fixed False Positive Rate (FPR=10⁻³): a CNN lens finder (Rezaei et al. 2022 architecture) is trained/evaluated separately per image type; TPR vs. Einstein radius is reported (Fig. 7). CLEAN-trained finder performance drops off below the ~3×PSF-FWHM image-separation limit found by Rezaei et al. (2022), consistent with prior literature. papers.title: A distributed resource-adaptive implementation of the widefield radio-interferometric measurement model for scalable image formation

runtime: Runtime breakdown by operation (Figure 8): FFT computations dominate total application runtime; de-gridding/gridding matrix-vector products are "almost negligible" by comparison; total application time grows with the number of w-layers (e.g., 23 → 126 layers).
iterations: Precomputation vs. application cost amortization: the one-off cost to build the operator matrix is matched by its application cost within "tens of iterations," and is exceeded by roughly an order of magnitude within a few hundred iterations of an iterative imaging algorithm — used as the basis for automatically choosing between precomputed and on-the-fly evaluation strategies.
compute_cost: Memory footprint of measurement matrices: explicit byte-cost formula for the de-gridding matrix, m_G(P) = 24K(P) + 4N′ bytes (K = non-zero elements, N′ = oversampled Fourier-space size), with an asymptotic regime m_G* ≈ 24MQ (M = number of measurements, Q = interpolation kernel support). Using the holographic-matrix (H) formulation instead of G gives a reported **7-fold reduction in memory** to store the operator, at roughly **30% higher precomputation cost**.

Precomputation vs. application cost amortization: the one-off cost to build the operator matrix is matched by its application cost within "tens of iterations," and is exceeded by roughly an order of magnitude within a few hundred iterations of an iterative imaging algorithm — used as the basis for automatically choosing between precomputed and on-the-fly evaluation strategies.

Number of w-layers / bins required (vs. WSClean baseline): used as a proxy for computational efficiency: e.g., 23 w-layers found optimal for a 10-node test configuration vs. WSClean's recommended 126 for pure w-stacking; 14 w-layers used for MeerKAT ESO 137-006 imaging (4096×4096 px, 1.91°) vs. WSClean's 40; 12 w-layers per frequency for an ASKAP field (4096×4096×8) vs. WSClean's 48–73. Fewer layers at comparable/better efficiency is the headline efficiency claim.

Distributed/parallel scaling: tested from 1 to 10 CPU nodes; the planning stage adapts the number of workers to available CPU cores (e.g., a 3-node run needing 122 workers but only 108 cores available triggers a switch to on-the-fly computation); inter-worker communication overhead (image-sized variable exchange with FFT workers, Fourier-coefficient exchange with de-gridding/gridding workers) is tracked as part of total cost.

Overall computational cost relative to CLEAN: for the MeerKAT ESO 137-006 case, the proposed high-precision measurement operator achieves imaging cost "within one order of magnitude of CLEAN," used as the headline scalability/cost comparison against the standard (non-ML) imaging pipeline.
